data.sourcePassage:
The transatlantic slave trade was one of the largest forced migrations in human history. Between the 1500s and 1800s, millions of African people were forcibly taken from their homes and transported across the Atlantic Ocean to the Americas. This was not accidental. It was organised for profit by European empires, merchants, shipowners, plantation owners and investors.

Africa was not a simple or undeveloped place. Before and during the slave trade, West and Central Africa contained many different kingdoms, cities, trading networks and skilled craftspeople. However, European demand for plantation labour, combined with competition and warfare within Africa, led some African rulers and merchants to become involved in selling captives. European empires created and expanded the Atlantic plantation system that made the trade grow to such a large scale.

The triangular trade connected Europe, Africa and the Americas. Ships carried manufactured goods such as textiles and guns from Europe to Africa, transported enslaved Africans across the Atlantic on what became known as the Middle Passage, and returned to Europe with plantation products such as sugar, tobacco and cotton.

Britain became deeply involved. Cities including Liverpool, Bristol, London and Glasgow grew wealthy through the trade and through connected industries such as shipbuilding, banking, insurance and sugar refining. By the 1700s, British merchants and ships were heavily involved in transporting enslaved Africans across the Atlantic.

questions.question: What was the Middle Passage?
options: A land route across Africa used by traders
The forced sea journey of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic
A passage in Parliament debating the slave trade
A canal connecting the Caribbean islands
questions.modelAnswer: The Middle Passage was the forced sea journey of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic Ocean from Africa to the Americas.

questions.question: According to the passage, which British cities grew wealthy through the slave trade?
options: Edinburgh, Cardiff, Manchester and Norwich
Liverpool, Bristol, London and Glasgow
York, Bath, Oxford and Cambridge
Portsmouth, Plymouth, Hull and Newcastle
questions.modelAnswer: Liverpool, Bristol, London and Glasgow are identified in the passage as British cities that grew wealthy through the slave trade and connected industries.

questions.question: Why does the passage say it is wrong to describe Africa as simple or undeveloped?
options: Because Africa was stronger than Europe at the time
Because West and Central Africa contained kingdoms, cities, trading networks and skilled craftspeople
Because all African rulers opposed the slave trade
Because Africa had already abolished slavery before Europeans arrived
questions.modelAnswer: The passage states that West and Central Africa contained many different kingdoms, cities, trading networks and skilled craftspeople, showing it was diverse and sophisticated.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the role of British industries beyond just plantation owners?
options: Only plantation owners in the Caribbean profited from slavery
British industries such as shipbuilding, banking and insurance were also connected to the slave trade
British industry was opposed to the slave trade from the beginning
Only traders in Africa benefited economically from slavery

data.sourcePassage:
After arrival in the Americas, enslaved people were sold at auctions or in private sales. Families could be separated. People were forced onto plantations, into homes, docks, workshops and mines. In the British Caribbean, sugar plantations were especially important. Sugar was difficult and dangerous to produce, involving planting, cutting cane, crushing it, boiling the juice and preparing it for export.

Plantation slavery depended on forced labour and brutal control. Enslavers used laws, punishment, surveillance and racist ideas to maintain power. They tried to control movement, family life, religion and education. Colonial laws treated enslaved people as property with little legal protection.

However, enslaved people were not passive victims. They resisted in many ways. Everyday resistance included slowing work, breaking tools, pretending not to understand orders and hiding food. Some ran away temporarily or permanently to form independent communities. Others organised revolts. Cultural survival was also vital: enslaved people preserved their names, music, religion, family bonds, stories and languages. This mattered because it protected identity and community against a system designed to reduce people to property.

The Haitian Revolution, beginning in 1791 in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, was the most dramatic example of resistance. Enslaved people fought and defeated French, British and Spanish forces. In 1804, Haiti became the first Black republic in the world. This revolutionary success frightened enslavers across the Atlantic and inspired anti-slavery movements everywhere.

options: Cotton
Sugar
Tobacco
Coffee
questions.modelAnswer: Sugar was especially important on British Caribbean plantations, requiring difficult and dangerous labour to produce.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is an example of everyday resistance by enslaved people?
options: Accepting all orders without question
Slowing work, breaking tools and hiding food
Investing in the plantation economy
Writing petitions to Parliament
questions.modelAnswer: Everyday resistance included slowing work, breaking tools, pretending not to understand orders and hiding food as ways of disrupting the plantation system.

questions.question: Why was cultural survival important for enslaved people?
options: It helped enslavers maintain control of the plantation
It protected identity and community against a system designed to reduce people to property
It was required by colonial law for enslaved people to maintain African practices
It had no significance and was simply entertainment

questions.question: Why was the Haitian Revolution so significant according to the passage?
options: Because it showed that only white abolitionists could end slavery
Because enslaved people defeated colonial forces and established the first Black republic, frightening enslavers and inspiring anti-slavery movements

Because it was the first example of resistance on a plantation

data.sourceTitle: The Abolition Movement and Its Impact
data.targetTitle: The Abolition Movement and Its Impact
data.sourcePassage:
Abolition in Britain was achieved through many causes working together. It cannot be credited to one person alone.

Black abolitionists and their testimony were central. Olaudah Equiano's 1789 autobiography described his enslavement and freedom, giving British readers direct evidence of the trade's cruelty. Ottobah Cugoano challenged slavery using moral arguments. Mary Prince's published testimony in 1831 exposed continuing violence in British colonies. Thomas Clarkson collected evidence, diagrams and objects that campaigners used in speeches and publications. William Wilberforce argued in Parliament, and Granville Sharp supported legal cases.

The campaign also involved boycotts, petitions and public meetings. Many ordinary people, including women who could not vote, participated in local campaigns to end the trade. Enslaved resistance was also crucial: revolts, escape and the Haitian Revolution weakened the plantation system and made slavery seem dangerous and unstable.

The 1807 Abolition of the Slave Trade Act ended British legal participation in transporting enslaved Africans. But slavery itself continued in British colonies. The 1833 Slavery Abolition Act ended legal slavery in most British colonies, coming into effect in 1834. However, formerly enslaved people were forced into 'apprenticeship', keeping them working for former enslavers. Full freedom came in 1838.

The 1833 settlement included £20 million paid to enslavers as compensation. Enslaved people received nothing. This reveals that abolition did not immediately create equality. Former enslavers kept land and wealth, while formerly enslaved people had to fight for wages, land, education, family stability and political rights. The legacy of slavery, including racism and wealth inequalities, continued long after abolition.

questions.question: What did the 1807 Abolition of the Slave Trade Act do?
options: It freed all enslaved people in British colonies immediately
It ended British legal participation in transporting enslaved Africans
It paid compensation to formerly enslaved people
It created the apprenticeship system
questions.modelAnswer: The 1807 Act ended British legal participation in transporting enslaved Africans, but did not free people already enslaved in British colonies.

questions.question: Why was the 1833 compensation settlement considered unfair?
options: Because it was paid to formerly enslaved people rather than to enslavers
Because enslavers received £20 million while enslaved people received nothing
Because the money was spent on building new plantations
Because it was paid to France rather than to British enslavers
questions.modelAnswer: The compensation settlement was unfair because £20 million was paid to enslavers for losing their 'property', while formerly enslaved people received nothing for their stolen lives and labour.

questions.question: According to the passage, why was enslaved resistance important to abolition?
options: Resistance had no impact on the plantation economy
Revolts and the Haitian Revolution weakened the plantation system and made slavery seem dangerous and unstable
Enslaved people persuaded Parliament to pass the 1807 Act directly
Resistance helped enslavers improve working conditions
questions.modelAnswer: Enslaved resistance was crucial because revolts, escape and the Haitian Revolution weakened the plantation system and made slavery seem dangerous and unstable to maintain.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the long-term legacy of slavery after abolition?
options: Abolition immediately created full equality and ended all racism
Racism and wealth inequalities continued, and formerly enslaved people had to fight for basic rights
Former enslavers lost all their land and wealth after 1833
The legacy of slavery had been fully resolved by the end of the Victorian period
questions.modelAnswer: The passage shows that abolition did not create immediate equality: former enslavers kept land and wealth, formerly enslaved people had to fight for basic rights, and the legacy of slavery including racism and wealth inequalities continued long after abolition.
